preamble: Deglottalization of the alveolar ejective [tʼ] to plain [t]. The clearest direct case is Geers's law in Akkadian: a root inherited with two emphatics (reconstructed as ejectives) keeps only one, and ṭ, the least stable in the hierarchy ṣ > ḳ > ṭ, becomes plain t next to ḳ or ṣ, while Arabic, Hebrew and Geʽez cognates keep both. The rule is usually explained by the cross-linguistic ban on two ejectives in one root (Bomhard & Kerns 1994; cf. MacEachern 1999 on laryngeal co-occurrence restrictions). Maltese, Cypriot Maronite Arabic and Modern Hebrew reach t in two steps, through pharyngealized tˤ (*tʼ > tˤ > t); each step is filed separately. Outside Semitic, stem-final *tʼ lost its glottalization in Lower Tanana, Tanacross, Deg Xinag and Navajo (Athabaskan), while Ahtna and Hupa keep it. In Chechen and Ingush, geminate *tʼː lost its glottalization but, unlike single non-initial tʼ (which became d), stayed voiceless.

examples.note: ṭ > t next to ṣ; Arabic ḍabaṭa and Hebrew ṣāḇaṭ keep both emphatics.
Arabic qaṭafa, Hebrew qāṭap, Syriac qṭap.
Geers's law also applies to loans: ṭ dissimilates and ḳ is kept (Streck 2011).
